title: Guided level 6 and 7 lab expansion
scope: Eight instructional exercises for owned/authorized practice or labeled simulation only
grading: Portfolio support only; no existing grade, completion or mastery records modified

labs.title: Virtual networking: isolated does not mean proven isolated
labs.environment: Owned VM network or Academy virtual-network simulator
labs.objective: Demonstrate that a vulnerable training guest cannot reach household resources while allowing an explicitly approved peer test.
labs.pre: Two fictional lab VMs: student 10.77.4.10/24 and service 10.77.4.20/24 on an internal switch. Household 192.168.1.0/24 is out of scope.
steps: Diagram connections
Record hypervisor adapter modes for each guest, each IP/subnet, the host's physical adapter and the intended boundary. Internal/host-only differs from bridged mode.
Observe guest IP and routes
On an owned Linux guest use ip -brief address and ip route; on Windows use ipconfig /all and route print. Identify active interfaces and default routes. Read-only first.
Validate approved path
Run ping -c 2 10.77.4.20 (Linux) or ping -n 2 10.77.4.20 (Windows) only after confirming this is your lab guest. A successful ping establishes limited ICMP reachability, not application health.
Validate isolation without probing private devices

Inspect adapter configuration, route tables and firewall policies; test a fictional denied route using the Academy simulation or a dedicated owned test endpoint. Do not send traffic to unapproved household devices.
Explain counterevidence
A private 10.x address alone does not prove isolation. NAT, forwarding or bridged interfaces can still allow paths; note any routes you could not independently test.
labs.evidence: Annotated network diagram, redacted adapter/route output, permitted connectivity results, denied-path evidence or simulation label, uncertainty and safe rollback.
labs.failure: Testing other people's devices, leaving a vulnerable guest bridged, or claiming isolation solely from a private IP.

labs.title: Service failure: distinguish listener, firewall and dependency
labs.environment: Disposable owned Linux VM or labeled Academy service simulation
labs.objective: Identify whether an owned practice web service is down, bound to loopback or filtered.
labs.pre: Fictional web service on owned guest 10.77.4.20:8000; client guest 10.77.4.10. Do not alter household infrastructure.
steps: Check service expectation
Record which service should run, its approved port, and what a successful response means before issuing commands.
Inspect read-only service state
Use systemctl status --no-pager <approved-service> and journalctl -u <approved-service> -n 20 --no-pager. If training without a real VM, interpret supplied sample logs.
Read listener binding
Use ss -ltn to distinguish 127.0.0.1:8000 from 0.0.0.0:8000 and 10.77.4.20:8000. A process can be running without accepting remote requests.
Test local and owned peer endpoints
Use curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8000 on the service guest and curl -I http://10.77.4.20:8000 on the approved peer. Compare refused, timeout, 200 and 404 outcomes.
Propose reversible correction
Describe whether an application bind, dependency or firewall policy is supported by evidence. Reconfigure only a disposable owned service with an approved rollback and rerun both tests.
labs.evidence: Baseline, two independent observations, hypothesis table, approved corrective change, positive/negative retest, rollback record.
labs.failure: Changing an unrelated service, interpreting HTTP 404 as no network connectivity, or asserting intrusion from one failed request.

labs.title: Snapshot recovery is not a backup
labs.environment: Owned disposable VM or simulation with a written recovery rehearsal
labs.objective: Verify repeatability and explain the shared failure domain of host-local snapshots.
labs.pre: Harmless test.txt with sample content and a named disposable VM checkpoint.
steps: Set baseline
Record VM identity, storage location, network mode, harmless service and sample file digest. Note secrets must not be embedded in exported evidence.
Create recovery point
Follow hypervisor documentation to capture a snapshot on an owned disposable guest; do not suspend or alter any production machine.
Introduce controlled change
Edit only the harmless test file or a temporary approved service setting, recording the original state.
Restore and verify
Restore the snapshot, repeat the file and service checks, confirm guest network isolation remains as expected, and log time required.
Identify failure modes
State what would be lost if the host SSD failed, and propose a separate controlled backup and restore test rather than claiming the snapshot is sufficient.
labs.evidence: Before/after checks, digest comparison, simulated or actual restore elapsed time, storage failure-domain diagram and restore limitations.
labs.failure: Calling snapshot presence a verified backup, skipping restored-system checks or using a non-disposable machine.

labs.title: Capacity planning for a low-cost workstation
labs.environment: Paper planning exercise using hypothetical Windows host hardware
labs.objective: Choose an achievable lab plan based on CPU virtualization, RAM, storage and upgrade limits.
labs.pre: Host scenarios: 4 GB RAM/64 GB storage and 16 GB RAM/512 GB SSD; requirements must be estimates, not vendor-certified measurements.
steps: Build resource ledger
Allocate memory and disk to the host OS before any guest; include realistic working reserves and storage expansion.
Choose lab mode
Explain why 4 GB hosts should use a browser simulator or one very small guest rather than several heavy desktop VMs.
Verify features
List BIOS virtualization support, RAM slot access, SSD expansion and supported hypervisors as items requiring exact model verification.
Model risk
Estimate concurrent VM memory demand and space for snapshots; mark uncertain inputs and avoid promising performance based only on core count.
Define pilot
Write a small initial test: one disposable guest, memory pressure observation, restore check and stop criteria if the host becomes unstable.
labs.evidence: Two-host comparison, explicit assumptions, resource spreadsheet, staged upgrade decision, risk and stop conditions.
labs.failure: Overcommitting guest RAM, assuming every desktop supports VT-x/AMD-V or assigning unverified performance claims.

labs.title: Rules of engagement and authorization boundary
labs.environment: Synthetic corporate exercise, no external scanning
labs.objective: Create a reviewable engagement plan that prevents scope drift.
labs.pre: Fictional Orion Group owns lab assets 10.77.4.10/24 and 10.77.4.20/24; the production 203.0.113.0/24 documentation range is explicitly excluded.
steps: Document owner and scope
Name a fictional owner, target inventory, permitted techniques, dates, data restrictions, emergency stop contact and approval evidence.
Test the boundary on paper
For five fictional targets, decide proceed / exclude / request new permission and explain each decision.
Choose observational methods
Prefer supplied synthetic system records and read-only owned VM checks. Avoid credential testing, third-party devices or exploitation outside the scenario.
Escalation drill
A simulated service outage occurs during a planned activity. Write a stop, preserve, report and rollback sequence.
Peer review
Have a reviewer challenge ambiguous terms like 'all company servers' and replace them with concrete identifiers and conditions.
labs.evidence: Rules-of-engagement document, target stop/go table, escalation sequence and explicit approval assumptions.
labs.failure: Treating related organizations or unlisted hosts as implicitly authorized.

labs.title: Detection hypotheses from messy evidence
labs.environment: Provided fictional authentication and reverse-proxy records
labs.objective: Distinguish raw events, duplicates and interpretive claims.
labs.pre: Synthetic logs: 09:02Z auth failure user-a src X; 09:02Z duplicate proxy 401 user-a src X; 09:05Z auth success user-a src X; 09:07Z service refresh user-b src Y. All identities fictional.
steps: Normalize
Create columns source, original timestamp, UTC, principal, event, outcome, record ID and confidence.
Correlate cautiously
Propose whether the first two records refer to one attempted action. Identify the fields that support or undermine correlation.
Form alternatives
Write two hypotheses for the 09:05 success: authorized user retry and possible misuse. Do not promote either to fact without more evidence.
Design safe test
Specify approved read-only identity/session and device-context records that could discriminate alternatives; never request passwords or tokens.
Write findings
Include a bounded conclusion, event gap/clock-skew limitations, severity rationale and one reviewer challenge.
labs.evidence: Normalized timeline, deduplication reasoning, alternate hypotheses, evidence limits and review-ready escalation note.
labs.failure: Declaring compromise from a failed-then-success pattern alone or copying actual credentials into reports.

labs.title: Remediation verification and regressions
labs.environment: Fictional private-record API or isolated owned demo
labs.objective: Construct a positive-and-negative authorization test plan and validate a remediation.
labs.pre: Synthetic API users student-a and student-b, record A owned by student-a; initial simulation wrongly allows student-b to read A.
steps: Capture baseline
Document exact authorization failure in the supplied synthetic trace, actor, affected object and expected access policy.
Define correction
State the trusted API check: authenticated principal must be authorized for the requested record and operation, not merely a hidden menu link.
Positive test
Expect student-a to access A after the change, using demo accounts and non-sensitive records.
Negative test
Expect student-b to be denied access to A and permitted to access only their own record.
Regression and rollback
Check normal application workflow, audit logging and safe restoration steps. Describe how a production report must distinguish simulation results from verified observations.
labs.evidence: Test matrix with expected and observed outcomes, API policy rationale, regression checks, scope and uncertainty.
labs.failure: Relying on CSS to enforce authorization or presenting demo test outcomes as production proof.

labs.title: Board-level security decision and evidence defense
labs.objective: Translate technical evidence into prioritized decisions with costs, ownership and uncertainty.
labs.pre: Synthetic corporate case: noisy authentication alerts, overly broad report-reader service identity and no tested recovery procedure.
steps: Separate issues
Create distinct findings for alert quality, access privilege and restore readiness. Do not merge all records into one 'breach' conclusion.
Rank risk
Assess exposure, plausible impact, confidence, affected workflow and time-to-fix; do not rely only on scanner score.
Offer choices
For each finding compare leave/monitor, scoped mitigation and broader redesign, including operational tradeoffs and residual risk.
Specify assurance
Set acceptance criteria: measured useful-alert rate, positive/negative least-privilege tests and a controlled restore transaction.
Defend
Write a two-minute executive brief plus a technical appendix. Identify two ways new evidence could change your recommendation.
labs.evidence: Executive summary, decision matrix, technical appendix, explicit assumptions and testable action owners.
labs.failure: Claiming zero residual risk, concealing evidence gaps or asserting a browser simulation proves operational deployment.
